entities.name: Ghibbelin of Arles
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ghibbelin of Sabran, known as Ghibbelin of Arles, was a pivotal figure in the ecclesiastical politics of the High Middle Ages, serving as Archbishop of Arles from 1080 to 1112, papal legate in the Levant from 1107 to 1108, and concurrently as the second Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem from 1108 until his death in 1112. His career spanned a critical period following the First Crusade, during which the Latin Church sought to consolidate its authority and presence in the newly established Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, making him a central administrator and diplomat in both Western Europe and the nascent Crusader States.

Ghibbelin's ascent began with his election as Archbishop of Arles, a significant see in the Kingdom of Burgundy, a territory then part of the Holy Roman Empire. He played an active role in the reform movement initiated by Pope Gregory VII and his successors, aligning himself with papal efforts to assert spiritual and temporal authority. His involvement in the First Crusade, though not as a military leader, positioned him for greater influence. In 1107, Pope Paschal II appointed him as a papal legate to the Holy Land, entrusting him with the delicate task of reorganizing the Latin Church in the Levant. This mission culminated in his election as Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem in 1108, succeeding Dagobert of Pisa, a controversial figure whose tenure was marked by conflict with King Baldwin I.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ghibbelin's dual role as Archbishop of Arles and Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem was crucial in establishing and defining the ecclesiastical structure of the Crusader States, shaping the relationship between secular and spiritual power in the Latin East for decades. His efforts helped to solidify the Latin Church's presence in the Levant following the First Crusade.
